title: Data, Lesson 4: Visualisation - picking the right chart, and spotting the one that lies
subtitle: Four questions that decide the chart type, and the axis tricks that make true numbers tell the wrong story
whyItMatters: A good chart shortens a meeting; a bad one drags it out. But more important than the skill of drawing is the skill of reading: you will constantly receive charts from other people - from broker reports to company presentations - and many of them are designed to lead you to a conclusion.
openingQuestion: Why is a vertical axis that does not start at 0 a problem on a bar chart?
openingOptions: Because charting software does not support the option
Because the eye reads bar height as an absolute value
Because the vertical axis must share the units of the horizontal one
Because it makes the chart hard to print on paper
explanation: On a bar chart the eye compares area and height, so a bar twice as tall is read as twice the value. Cutting the axis at 95 makes the step from 96 to 98 look like a tripling, when in reality it is barely two per cent. Note that the rule is different for line charts: a line represents a trend rather than a magnitude, so cutting the axis to make the movement visible is usually acceptable - as long as it is labelled clearly.

diagram.label: Relationship between two variables: a scatter
Distribution of one variable: a histogram

realWorldExample.company: The growth chart in a fundraising deck
realWorldExample.description: One very common shape: monthly revenue plotted with a vertical axis starting just below the smallest value, so the line looks almost vertical. The data is entirely real and nothing is falsified, but the visual impression describes a growth rate quite different from the numbers. The fastest check when you receive a chart like this: read the vertical axis label before you look at the shape of the line.

quiz.question: When should you use a scatter plot rather than a bar chart?
options: When the data contains negative values that bars cannot represent clearly
When the number of groups to compare has passed ten and bars get crowded
When you need to show the relationship between two continuous variables
When you want to emphasise the single largest value in the dataset being presented
quiz.explanation: A scatter is the only tool for the question of how two variables move together. It also reveals things a correlation coefficient hides, such as a curved relationship or data splitting into two clusters. Bars handle negatives perfectly well, crowding is solved by a horizontal bar chart, and highlighting a maximum is a formatting choice rather than a reason to change chart type.

quiz.question: Why are pie charts usually discouraged?
options: Because the slices in a pie chart do not always add up to exactly one hundred
Because a pie chart cannot represent percentage values below one per cent
Because a pie needs more colours and is harder to print on a black and white printer
Because the eye compares angles and areas far less accurately than lengths
quiz.explanation: With two or three clearly different slices a pie is fine. The problem appears when there are seven or eight nearly equal parts - at that point a horizontal bar chart sorted by size is far easier to read. Slices do sum to the whole by construction, small percentages can be shown with labels, and printing is a production concern rather than a perceptual one.

quiz.question: What question does a histogram answer that the mean does not?
options: How the data is distributed: concentrated, skewed to one side, or split into clusters
Which value in the dataset is the largest and which one happens to be the smallest
How many observations were missing data in the column currently under examination
How strongly the two variables in the dataset are related to one another overall
quiz.explanation: Two datasets with the same mean can have entirely different shapes. Drawing a histogram before reporting any mean at all is a habit worth having. The maximum and minimum are two numbers rather than a shape, missing data is a data quality question, and any measure of association needs two variables where a histogram takes one.

quiz.question: You receive a line chart rising steeply. What is the first thing to do?
options: Check whether the author used enough distinct colours to separate the lines
Read the label and the value range on the vertical axis before judging the shape
Count the data points on the line to be sure the sample is large enough to conclude
Ask the sender to supply an additional bar chart showing the same set of figures
quiz.explanation: The axis is the first place to look and the last place people look. A truncated axis or an unlabelled logarithmic scale is enough to change the story the picture tells completely. Colour is irrelevant on a single line, counting points does not tell you the scale, and asking for a second chart delays a check you can do in two seconds.

quiz.question: You receive a bar chart showing a very large gap. What should you check first?
options: Whether every bar in the chart has been given a complete label
Which source the data came from and how recently it was updated
Whether the vertical axis starts at zero or has been cut
Whether there are enough bars to make the trend visible
quiz.explanation: On a bar chart the eye reads height as value, so truncating the axis is the cheapest and most common distortion. Note that this rule does not carry over to line charts - there the eye reads the slope, and forcing the axis to zero can make a real movement disappear. Labels and sourcing matter, but neither one changes what the picture appears to say.

keyTakeaways: The question decides the chart type: comparison, trend, relationship or distribution
A bar chart must start at 0; a line chart need not, but say so clearly
A pie chart is only fine with few parts and clear differences between them
Draw a histogram before reporting any mean
When you receive someone else's chart, read the axis before you look at the shape

practicePrompt.question: You need to present the revenue share of 9 product lines, several of them close in size. Which chart do you choose?
options: A pie chart, since this is the share of a single whole
A horizontal bar chart sorted in descending order, with percentage labels
A line chart connecting the shares of the 9 product lines
A scatter plot with product names on the horizontal axis
practicePrompt.explanation: It is share data, true, but with nine nearly equal parts the eye cannot rank the slices. Horizontal bars allow comparison by length - the thing the eye does best - and long product names remain readable. A line chart is wrong in substance: joining discrete products with a line implies a continuity between them that does not exist.

summary.keyIdea: The question chooses the chart, not the other way round
summary.commonMistake: Choosing a chart type out of habit or because it looks attractive, then forcing the data into it
summary.action: Before you draw, write down the question you want this picture to answer. If you cannot write it, the chart is not needed yet.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Take three charts from any analyst report and for each one answer: where does the vertical axis start, does the chart type suit the question, and if you switched to another type would the conclusion change with it?
application.secondary: Reading other people's charts sceptically is the fastest way to draw better ones yourself.

sections.text: Visualisation is not a decorative final step. It is the step where you decide what the reader will see first - and in many cases that is the only thing they will remember.

sections.title: Choose by the question, not by habit
sections.subtitle: Pin down the question first and the chart type more or less presents itself

concepts.def: A bar chart. The value axis must start at 0, because the eye reads bar height as absolute magnitude.
A line chart. Here the axis need not start at 0, because what matters is direction and slope rather than magnitude.
A scatter plot. It reveals what a correlation coefficient conceals: curved relationships, separate clusters, dominant outliers.
A histogram or a box plot. It answers the question the mean cannot: how the data is actually spread out.

left.label: An honest chart
left.text: The axis states its units and its range clearly. Bars start at 0. Any logarithmic scale is spelled out. Just enough colours to distinguish the series, no more.

right.label: Signs to be wary of
right.text: A truncated vertical axis with no note. Two vertical axes on different scales side by side. A time window that conveniently starts at the bottom. Three-dimensional effects that distort the proportions.

sections.label: Dual axes: the hardest trick to spot
sections.text: Putting two lines on one picture with two different scales lets the author manufacture almost any degree of apparent agreement between the two quantities - all it takes is adjusting the scales until the lines touch at a few points. The viewer sees a tight relationship the data itself never asserted. When you meet a dual-axis chart, redraw each line on its own before believing the connection.

lines: Charts do not lie with wrong numbers. They lie with the axis, with the time window and with the type chosen.
The next lesson moves from a single chart to a collection of them: the dashboard.
